metadata.title: Autonomic dysfunction in stiff person syndrome (SPS): Observations in 8 cases
metadata.abstract: Objectives: Describe autonomic involvement in 8 consecutive patients with stiff person syndrome Background: SPS is mediated by antibodies to the glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) enzyme. In addition to muscle stiffness and pain, patients may present with: cerebellar symptoms, progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM), multifocal presentations with rigidity, epilepsy and brainstem signs, limbic encephalitis, downbeat nystagmus. In multifocal cases symptoms of paroxysmal dysautonomia have been described. Method(s): Retrospective review of a series of consecutive SPS cases seen over the past 2 years. All patients underwent clinical evaluations, laboratory testing, GAD 65 antibody testing, electrophysiological testing (6 out of 8 patients) and autonomic testing. Autonomic testing included measurement of postganglionic sudomotor function (QSWEAT), heart rate to deep breathing, heart rate and blood pressure responses to the Valsalva maneuver and head up tilt table testing. Result(s): There were 3 men (average age 43) and 5 women (average age 51). Average time from symptom onset to diagnosis was 2 years for men and 6 years for women. Only one case (male) was antibody negative. Autonomic symptoms: 6 patients had sweating abnormalities, 5 patients had lower GI symptoms, 2 had upper GI symptoms: one gastroparesis and one progressive dysphagia, 5 had mild orthostatic intolerance and one had syncope, 3 had palpitations and 2 had urinary symptoms. Abnormalities on autonomic testing included: cardiovagal dysfunction in 3, orthostatic tachycardia in 3, combination of sympathetic vasomotor and cardiac sympathetic hypofunction in 2 and one patient had a length dependent sudomotor loss pattern. Conclusion(s): Autonomic involvement is not rare, may not just be paroxysmal and may occur early in the course of SPS. Autonomic involvement may be a clue to the diagnosis particularly in patients with only mild stiffness and pain..

Poster 20
Autonomic dysfunction in stiff person syndrome (SPS):
observations in 8 cases
A. Barboi
Department of Neurological Sciences, Rush University, Chicago, IL,
USA
Objectives: Describe autonomic involvement in 8 consecutive
patients with stiff person syndrome
Background: SPS is mediated by antibodies to the glutamic acid
decarboxylase (GAD) enzyme. In addition to muscle stiffness and
pain, patients may present with: cerebellar symptoms, progressive
encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM), multifocal
presentations with rigidity, epilepsy and brainstem signs, limbic
encephalitis, downbeat nystagmus. In multifocal cases symptoms of
paroxysmal dysautonomia have been described.
Methods: Retrospective review of a series of consecutive SPS cases
seen over the past 2 years. All patients underwent clinical evalua-
tions, laboratory testing, GAD 65 antibody testing,
electrophysiological testing (6 out of 8 patients) and autonomic
testing. Autonomic testing included measurement of postganglionic
sudomotor function (QSWEAT), heart rate to deep breathing, heart
rate and blood pressure responses to the Valsalva maneuver and head
up tilt table testing.
Results: There were 3 men (average age 43) and 5 women (average
age 51). Average time from symptom onset to diagnosis was 2 years
for men and 6 years for women. Only one case (male) was antibody
negative. Autonomic symptoms: 6 patients had sweating abnormali-
ties, 5 patients had lower GI symptoms, 2 had upper GI symptoms:
one gastroparesis and one progressive dysphagia, 5 had mild ortho-
static intolerance and one had syncope, 3 had palpitations and 2 had
urinary symptoms. Abnormalities on autonomic testing included:
cardiovagal dysfunction in 3, orthostatic tachycardia in 3, combina-
tion of sympathetic vasomotor and cardiac sympathetic hypofunction
in 2 and one patient had a length dependent sudomotor loss pattern.
Conclusions: Autonomic involvement is not rare, may not just be
paroxysmal and may occur early in the course of SPS. Autonomic
involvement may be a clue to the diagnosis particularly in patients
with only mild stiffness and pain.

A comparison of the progression of autonomic dysfunction
in diabetic patients compared to other etiologies
J.L. Gilden, C. Prades, S. Paturi, I. Worden, C. Xiang, B. Theckedath,
J. Stoll, R. Trotta
Department of Medicine/Diabetes and Endocrinology, Rosalind
Franklin University of Medicine and Science/Chicago Medical
School and Captain James A. Lovell Federal Health Care Center,
North Chicago, IL, USA
QT intervals, which represent electrical depolarization and repolari-
zation of the ventricles, corrected for heart rate intervals (QTc) on
electrocardiograms, can be used as a surrogate marker for progression
of autonomic neuropathy (AN) over time in diabetic patients (DM).
Evaluation of the utility of QTc as a measure in patients with other
etiologies of AN, identiﬁed by those with neurogenic orthostatic
hypotension (NOH) (decrease in blood pressure with inadequate heart
rate response upon upright posture and symptoms of dizziness/light-
headedness, visual disturbances, presyncope/syncope) has not been
well established. Therefore, we compared QTc interval prolongation
over an average time period of 7.6 ± 7.06 years in DM vs. NOH by
retrospective chart review of 87 subjects [(47 DM : 7 Type 1: 40 Type
2;) (Hgba1c = 7.3 ± 1.8 %))(40 NOH; 24 PAF:5 AI : 3 MSA: 5 PD:
3 other) (BMI = 30.5 ± 5.8 kg/m
2)]. QTc values were determined
using the standard formula of Bazett. Results: The mean values for
QTc at baseline were not signiﬁcantly different between the two
groups (434 ± 28 vs. 430 ± 34 ms). Although both groups demon-
strated worsening of AN over time, with more prolongation of QTc
for the NOH group (434 ± 26 vs. 440 ± 28 ms; p \ 0.001), the
NOH group also had a greater decline when each subject was com-
pared to their own baseline (0.53 vs. 22; p \ 0.001). This was also
conﬁrmed by comparing slopes for the line of best ﬁt (DM = 0.1396
vs. NOH = 1.012; p \ 0.001). Co-morbid conditions of migraine,
fatigue, ﬁbromyalgia, palpitations, and exercise intolerance were
signiﬁcantly greater for NOH than DM (p \ 0.001), except that for
hypoglycemia. Thus, although there was prolongation of the QTc
interval over time in both DM and other etiologies of autonomic
dysfunction, the NOH subjects demonstrated a more rapid and further
decline of autonomic function.
This research is supported, in part, by the JAL FHCC.
Poster 22
Prolonged QTc interval in patients seropositive for ganglionic
(a-3) acetylcholine receptor autoantibody
W.P. Cheshire, K.L. Venkatachalam, M.H. Yamani, V.A. Lennon
Departments of Neurology, Cardiology, and Immunology, Mayo
Clinic, Jacksonville, FL, and Rochester, MN, USA
Background: The clinical presentations of patients with ganglionic
(a3) acetylcholine receptor autoantibodies ( a3-AChR-Ab) are
diverse. We encountered a seropositive patient who acquired unex-
plained long QT interval that led to ventricular ﬁbrillation and sudden
cardiac death. She was successfully resuscitated. We therefore sought
to determine whether there might be an unrecognized association
between this cardiac arrhythmia and ganglionic a3-AChR-Ab.
Methods: We reviewed retrospectively medical records of all patients
seen at Mayo Clinic in Florida (2007–2013) who were tested for
a3-AChR-Ab and had an electrocardiogram within 1 year of antibody
testing. Using analysis of variance and linear regression, we compared
QTc intervals derived by Bazett’s formula and corrected for QRS
duration for antibody-positive patients ( [0.02 nmol/L) and an equal
number of antibody-negative patients.
Results: Of 146 a3-AChR-Ab-positive patients (median age 61 years,
range 18–92; 55 % female), 107 had an electrocardiogram within 1 year.
Sixty-three patients had low antibody values (0.03–0.09 nmol/L), 38
medium (0.10–0.99 nmol/L), and 6 high (C1.00 nmol/L). Mean QTc for
women was 446 ± 33 ms (antibody-positive) versus 432 ± 24 ms
(antibody-negative; p = 0.01). Mean QTc for men was 430 ± 35 ms
(antibody-positive) versus 434± 39 ms (antibody-negative; p = 0.59).
Although antibody values and QTc did not correlate signiﬁcantly, QT
intervals were generally longer in women with medium or higha3-AChR-
Ab values than in seronegative patients (33 versus 7 %, Fischer’s exact
test p = 0.06).
Conclusions: a3-AChR-antibody status correlated signiﬁcantly with
prolonged QTc interval in female but not male patients. The apparent
lack of dose-dependence of this newly recognized, but infrequent,
accompaniment of autoimmune autonomic ganglionopathy suggests
that its occurrence may depend on epitope or IgG class. Our ﬁndings
justify adding a3-AChR-Ab to the list of autoantibodies implicated in
the pathogenesis of cardiac dysrhythmias. We hypothesize that
autoimmune disruption of a3-ACh receptors in intracardiac neurons
